The Perils of Potent Pot Party Line: Blaming Marijuana Legalization for Increase in THC Levels

There is a line from one of the James Bond novels where Bond says, “Once is an accident. Twice is a coincidence. Three times is enemy action.”

Well, maybe marijuana has made me paranoid, or maybe it’s fifty years of lying narcs, pseudo-science, or thirty million arrests, but…

Recently, there has been a spate of articles in otherwise respectable publications warning that cannabis is much stronger (has more THC), therefore “much more dangerous than it used to be way back when everyone thought it was harmless.”

THC, Tetrahydrocannabinol, is the principal psychoactive ingredient in cannabis, which wasn’t discovered until 1964 in Israel (three years before I “discovered” it in Texas).

In 2023, New Scientist magazine published a really comprehensive history of THC levels in cannabis:

“Is cannabis today really much more potent than 50 years ago?”

New Scientist article

Yes.

“Levels of the psychoactive compound THC have been steadily rising in marijuana since the 1970s, due largely to growers selecting for more potent strains.”

I will be writing more about the other articles soon, but the New Scientist article offers much more data.

First, let me say that I am pleased to report that the quality of cannabis has improved enormously over the last 58 years. We definitely got high in the sixties, but it is actually much safer today,  where it is legal.

And I am also proud to say that I have smoked “Haze” with the late Nevil Schoenmakers and “Skunk” with the late David Watson, and other beautiful flowers with many other talented breeders/gardeners over the years.

As best I can remember.

The point is that they have all improved an enormously valuable plant that has helped many more people than it has harmed and saved many lives.

Of course, the Prohibitionists tried to destroy it. But that’s a story for another time. Soon.

In any case, this article also shows the influence of the Prohibitionists’ party line, complaining that more and more people think that it is “relatively harmless.”

Relatively harmless? So is cannabis relatively less harmless now, when we can know the THC levels?

First, the argument for legalization has never been based on claims that cannabis is “harmless,” because nothing is harmless for everyone, in all doses, and under all circumstances. And “harmlessness” is not a qualification for anything.

Relative to what?

To alcohol? CDC: Alcohol Facts

“Excessive alcohol use is a leading preventable cause of death in the United States. About 178,000 people die from excessive drinking each year. These deaths occur from both drinking alcohol over several years or drinking too much on one occasion.”

To tobacco? From American Lung Association: Smoking Facts

“Smoking is the number one preventable cause of death in the U.S., killing over 490,000 people per year.”

To benzodiazepines available by prescription?

“A total of 118,208 benzodiazepine-involved overdose deaths occurred between 2000 and 2019.” PubMed: Benzodiazepine Overdose Deaths 

Relatively harmless?

And is Marijuana Prohibition harmless, with 30 million arrests and continuing at over 200,000 per year?

No one even tries to figure out the health consequences of that.

What I find most annoying about this latest version of “the latest research” is that I was writing about this in 1998.

This is perhaps the simplest and yet most important example of why I say that “bad journalism” is the best two-word explanation of Marijuana Prohibition.

Stop the presses! The LATEST RESEARCH!!!!!

From 1998: The Prohibitionists in Stockholm Reveal the Shocking Truth About the Potency of Dutch Marijuana Read it here

Of course, Dutch THC levels have risen since then.

And from 1999: Minneapolis Prohibitionist Opposes Hemp Cultivation, Says “The marijuana smoked at Woodstock contained ‘industrial hemp’ levels of THC.” See the Punch Line at the End Read it here

The point here is simply that the Prohibitionists have been using this “latest research” as a reason to keep cannabis in the black market for decades.

The fundamental fallacies in the “potent pot perils” are really embarrassingly obvious.

First, cannabis has never come in standard dosages with an implied level of THC. There has always been extreme variability in strength, but we just had no way of knowing. I may or may not have smoked “Acapulco Gold” — but, as someone observed, the sixties were definitely not about a placebo.

When cannabis is contraband, as it still is in most of the world, there is no way of knowing the “potency.” Also, there is no way of knowing the level of CBD, or other cannabinoids. (Or contaminants.)

Second, cannabis users have always adjusted their dosage sizes from the beginning, based on their personal preferences, the perceived strength, and their manner of consuming—whether bongs, vaporizers, pipe bowls, even one called a “one-hitter,” or “joints” that could be a “fatty” or a “pinner,” etc. etc.

Think of all the different sizes of glasses in a typical bar. There are sizes from single shot glasses to tumblers.

Of course, back when alcohol was contraband in a “speakeasy,” you couldn’t know how much ethanol you were drinking, or even be sure that it wasn’t highly toxic methanol. An estimated 50,000 Americans died of methanol poisoning during alcohol Prohibition. Relatively harmless?

Also, under prohibition, the economics of contraband encourage the consumer to buy—or dealers to sell—“stronger” products. See Iron Law of Prohibition

It is actually the black market that makes anything more dangerous, especially for adolescents because they don’t know what they are getting—or even if it is really cannabis, as opposed to “synthetic marijuana,” which isn’t really cannabis at all and is actually very dangerous.

Obviously, there has to be a legal minimum age, but the higher it is, the closer young people are to the dangers of the black market, and the further they are from regulation.

The purported increase in mental health problems in teens who have reportedly used cannabis may or may not demonstrate that cannabis is a higher risk for them—but it definitely demonstrates that making it illegal for them did not protect them.

In The Netherlands, where cannabis has been sold over the counter for almost fifty years, the legal age is eighteen. It used to be sixteen, and former Dutch Justice Minister Piet Donner, who raised the minimum age, later said that he thought it was a mistake. And the Dutch rate of cannabis use is less than half that of the U.S.

Meanwhile, in every state, ethanol—the active ingredient in wine, beer, and cocktails—is available in packages up to 95% potency. A relatively small dose of that could be fatal.

As for blaming legalization for the increase in potency, remember—as the New Scientist article demonstrates—the government’s own data shows that it has been increasing for fifty years. Legal limits on THC levels would be a subsidy to the black market and increase whatever dangers there are in contraband products.

So why isn’t cannabis regulated like alcohol? Then the Prohibitionists can try to bring back alcohol prohibition. It only lasted 13 years, unlike cannabis prohibition, which has been rolling along for almost eighty-eight years.

Maybe if we had just tried for another century.

Actually, cannabis is an enormously complex plant, and as Dr. Peter Grinspoon explains: “Today’s Weed Is Incredibly Strong. But That’s Not What You Should Be Worried About. Politicians are fearmongering about marijuana potency—and they’re about to make things worse.”

To paraphrase Jefferson, the politicians who regulate least, regulate best.
